To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) we find that a user's behavior on one site is often correlated with her behavior on another site; 2) we find that even very weak correlations are often sufficient to de-anonymize users; and 3) we find that users are often willing to disclose more personal information on one site than on another site, which makes it easier for us to de-anonymizing users.
We show that subtle correlations in a person's activity patterns across multiple social computing sites can be used to de-anonymize a user with a high degree of accuracy.

(i) even very weak signals, such as the similarity of a user's textual content across platforms, can be used for accurate de-anonymizations, and (ii) de-anonymizations based on weak signals can be used for privacy-invasive attacks, but can also be useful for privacy-protecting purposes.
